builder_plan.scenario: An assistant chooses the wrong API or sends arguments your product cannot use.
builder_plan.change: Apply the proposed tool-selection or argument-generation change in a sandbox.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current agent with the same tool schemas and task budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Correct completed actions, invalid calls, retries, latency, and cost per completed task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model
summary: The method replaces both unverified in-network arithmetic (sampled accuracy with no per-input guarantee) and calculator-style tool calls, by having a small adapted model execute procedures step-by-step on a rendered external sheet whose correctness over a finite view set is machine-checked. It costs a custom training adapter, a dedicated rendering and runtime stack, formal verification effort, and many sequential forward passes per operation, so latency scales with problem length far worse than a single tool call. Adoption fails if any of the finite views fails certification on the deployment quantization, if workloads need operations outside the verified procedure set, or if the added per-step inference latency outweighs the value of in-network exactness over calling a calculator.
rationale: The formal exactness guarantee is genuinely novel, but for a constrained production team the same exactness is obtained more cheaply and reliably by routing arithmetic to a deterministic tool, while this approach requires adapter training, a rendering runtime, and verification infrastructure with no latency or cost advantage.
technique: Certified exact arithmetic via bounded-view external memory

claims.statement: The method replaces both unverified in-network arithmetic (sampled accuracy with no per-input guarantee) and calculator-style tool calls, by having a small adapted model execute procedures step-by-step on a rendered external sheet whose correctness over a finite view set is machine-checked. It costs a custom training adapter, a dedicated rendering and runtime stack, formal verification effort, and many sequential forward passes per operation, so latency scales with problem length far worse than a single tool call. Adoption fails if any of the finite views fails certification on the deployment quantization, if workloads need operations outside the verified procedure set, or if the added per-step inference latency outweighs the value of in-network exactness over calling a calculator.

Certified-exact model solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems and 220 of 220 long sums and products, versus 217 of 220 for the strongest of ten comparison models; the paper's central claim is a formal (Lean-proved) exactness guarantee on all inputs, not a rate improvement.
